rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The play at a glance "Facing Death" by August Strindberg is a naturalist one-act tragedy about a man destroyed by the way the world sees him — and redeemed, at the last minute, by what he actually does. Monsieur Durand, a widowed ex-railway man running a failing pension, is regarded by his three daughters and the town as a drunkard, a gambler and a failure.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Monsieur Durand sacrifices his reputation for his daughters — hidden nobility.
Tragic irony: the family despises him while he provides; discuss the poison decision.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: The daughters' contempt softens too late — the recognition scene is the emotional climax; quote the moment of pity.  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **Monsieur Durand** is the play's paradox: a man who must be despised to be generous. His weakness for display, his drinking, his evasions — some real, some performed — are the mask over the plan, and his last hours reveal the truth the mask hid: a father who loved his daughters enough to be hated by them. The character sketch the exam wants holds both readings at once.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **Sacrifice and misjudgment** — the central theme: the sacrifice that must disguise itself as failure; the play asks what it costs to be good when goodness cannot be explained. **Appearance versus truth** — the conceptual heart: the town's and the daughters' verdicts are built from surfaces, and the truth was invisible by design.…  ·  ## NEB short answers, solved **Q. What is Durand's situation at the start of the play? (2 marks)** A. Ruined and despised: the pension he runs is mortgaged and failing, his debts are pressing, and his three daughters — taught by the town's verdict — regard him as a drunkard, a gambler and a failure. The setup is a man judged entirely by his surfaces. **Q. How do the daughters treat their father? (2 marks)** A.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. Why does Durand poison himself? (2 marks) — his life insurance is the only way to provide for his daughters.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ## NEB long answers, solved **Q. "Durand must be despised in order to be generous." Discuss the paradox at the heart of the play. (8 marks)** A model answer works the paradox structurally and morally: the insurance pays only on death, so the plan requires concealment — every explanation would forfeit the provision — and Durand therefore performs the failure the town expects, letting the swagger and the drinking…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The action, scene by scene The setup is a portrait of ruin: the pension is mortgaged and failing, Durand is behind on everything, and his three daughters — raised to despise him — treat him with the contempt the town has taught them. The exposition is brutal and efficient: we learn of the dead wife, the drinking, the debts, and the daughters' conviction that their father is the source of every shame.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Naturalism** — the play's master mode: heredity, poverty and social judgment as the forces that crush the man; no providence, no melodrama — the tragedy is economic and psychological, room by room. - **Dramatic irony** — the play's engine: the audience shares the daughters' contempt until the truth surfaces, and the reversal re-colours every earlier scene — the swagger was a…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Monsieur Durand's sacrifice: he poisons himself to leave insurance money for his daughters — the tragic irony of buying love with death; state it.  ·  Trick 2: His flaws caused the fall (temper, debts, lost hotel) — character-driven tragedy; trace cause to effect in two steps.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. What is tragic about Durand's character? (2 marks) — pride and temper ruined him, yet he dies for the family that despises him.
